messages.content: You help health workers apply the IMCI chart booklet for children aged 2 months to 5 years. Always check danger signs before anything else, and refer urgently when in doubt. You give protocol-following decision support, not a diagnosis.

I brought my child in today. The child is about 8 months old. No ear problem. We came by bus this morning. There is chest indrawing. She coughs and struggles to breathe. She hasn't had diarrhoea. Her brother had the same thing. Sixty-five breaths per minute. She hasn't had a fever. Please tell me what to do.

CLASSIFICATION: MODERATE — Pneumonia (IMCI yellow: treat and follow up)

WHY: No general danger signs were found, so the assessment continues by symptom. There is chest indrawing. The respiratory rate is 65 breaths per minute. For a child of 8 months the fast-breathing threshold is 50, so this counts as fast breathing.
ACTION: Give oral Amoxicillin for 5 days. Soothe throat/relieve cough. Advise mother when to return immediately. Follow-up in 3 days.
DOSING: amoxicillin 1 x 250 mg tablet (or 5 ml of 250 mg/5 ml syrup), two times daily for 5 days

This follows the published IMCI algorithm and does not replace a clinician. When the picture is unclear, refer.

We walked here from the next village. Chidi is 1 year and 8 months old. It rained all night. Her brother had the same thing. There's something wrong with her ear. There's a tender swelling behind her ear. Breathing is fine.

CLASSIFICATION: SEVERE — Mastoiditis (IMCI pink: refer urgently)

WHY: No general danger signs were found, so the assessment continues by symptom. There is tender swelling behind the ear, which indicates mastoiditis.
ACTION: Give first dose of antibiotic and paracetamol for pain. Refer URGENTLY.
DOSING: ceftriaxone 750 mg (3 ml) IM; paracetamol 1 x 100 mg tablet, every 6 hours until fever or pain settles

Protocol-following guidance only — not a diagnosis. The chart booklet and your own clinical judgment come first, and referral is always the safe choice when unsure.

Sorry to bother you. Ngozi is 26 months old. I've been giving him water. He isn't coughing. He was fine last week. His temperature is up. No neck stiffness. Should I take him to the hospital?

CLASSIFICATION: MODERATE — Fever, malaria not yet assessed (IMCI yellow: treat and follow up)

WHY: No general danger signs were found, so the assessment continues by symptom. The child has fever, with no stiff neck and no general danger signs. Note that this assessment does not cover malaria risk or a malaria test, which the chart booklet requires for any child with fever.
ACTION: Give paracetamol for high fever. Assess malaria risk and test per the chart booklet, then treat according to the result. Refer for assessment if the fever persists more than 7 days, and advise the mother when to return immediately.
DOSING: paracetamol 1 x 100 mg tablet, every 6 hours until fever or pain settles
NOTE: There is also an ear complaint. Fever is assessed before ear problems, so deal with this classification first and then check the ear.

CLASSIFICATION: SEVERE — Severe dehydration (young infant) (IMCI pink: refer urgently)

WHY: There is diarrhoea with the infant is less than 1 month old, which is severe dehydration in a young infant.
ACTION: Start intravenous fluids (Plan C). Give the first dose of an intramuscular antibiotic. Keep the infant warm on the way to hospital. Refer URGENTLY.

Doctor, Blessing is twelve months old. She can't get enough to drink. The diarrhoea has been going for 19 days. Blessing has watery stools. The eyes look fine. Her brother had the same thing. It rained all night. She keeps crying and fussing. The skin pinch goes back slowly. Is it serious?

CLASSIFICATION: MODERATE — Some dehydration (IMCI yellow: treat and follow up)

WHY: No general danger signs were found, so the assessment continues by symptom. Signs of some dehydration are present: restless or irritable, drinks eagerly, thirsty and skin pinch goes back slowly. Two or more of the four classify as some dehydration.
ACTION: Give fluid, zinc, and food for some dehydration (Plan B). Follow-up in 5 days if not improving.
DOSING: zinc 1 x 20 mg tablet daily for 14 days
ALSO: persistent diarrhoea (>=14 days) -- multivitamins/zinc for 14 days, follow-up 5 days
NOTE: The child also has a fever. Classify the diarrhoea first as the booklet orders, then come back to the fever.

Decision support, not a diagnosis: always confirm against the IMCI chart booklet and refer if anything is in doubt.

ACTION: Give vitamin A. Advise the mother when to return immediately.
DOSING: vitamin A 200,000 IU

Good morning. The child is just over 2 years old. The MUAC measures 110 millimetres. Weight-for-height is -3.5 z-scores. What should I do?

CLASSIFICATION: MODERATE — Uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition (IMCI yellow: treat and follow up)

WHY: Weight-for-height is -3.5 z-scores, below -3. MUAC is 110mm, below 115mm. The appetite test passed and there is no medical complication.
ACTION: Give ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) for the child to take at home. Assess and counsel on feeding. Advise the mother when to return immediately. Follow up in 7 days.
DOSING: amoxicillin 3 x 250 mg tablet (or 15 ml of 250 mg/5 ml syrup), two times daily for 5 days; vitamin A 200,000 IU

CLASSIFICATION: MILD — Cough or cold (IMCI green: home care)

WHY: No general danger signs were found, so the assessment continues by symptom. There is no fast breathing, no chest indrawing, and no stridor, so this is a simple cough or cold rather than pneumonia.
ACTION: Soothe the throat, relieve cough with a safe remedy. Advise mother when to return immediately. Follow-up in 5 days if not improving.

WHY: The child is HIV-exposed: on ARV prophylaxis, or with a negative test while still breastfeeding or within 6 weeks of breastfeeding, so infection is not yet ruled out.
ACTION: Complete the appropriate infant ARV prophylaxis. Repeat HIV PCR testing per the schedule and reclassify on the result. Ask about the caregiver's health and provide follow-up care.

WHY: A generalised rash with cough, runny nose, or red eyes meets the measles case definition. There is a general danger sign, deep or extensive mouth ulcers, which makes this severe complicated measles.
ACTION: Give vitamin A. Give the first dose of an appropriate antibiotic. If there is clouding of the cornea or pus draining from the eye, apply tetracycline eye ointment. Refer URGENTLY to hospital.
DOSING: vitamin A 100,000 IU; amoxicillin 1 x 250 mg tablet (or 5 ml of 250 mg/5 ml syrup), two times daily for 5 days
